title: Serving with vLLM — three techniques
intro: The GPU should never wait for work, and no cache byte should sit reserved for a token that never comes.

steps.title: The GPU is starving
steps.body: Decode is **bandwidth-bound**: every step streams all the weights from HBM while the tensor cores idle. The compute per token is tiny; the data movement is the bill. **Batching** reads the weights once for many users — same movement, many tokens:

viz.title: The token factory
viz.caption: Watch 'GPU doing math %' climb as the batch grows — the cores finally stop waiting.

steps.title: Continuous beats static
steps.body:
**Static** batching schedules whole batches — fine when outputs are fixed-size (BERT, YOLO), terrible for LLMs where "what's 2+2" shares a batch with a 2000-word essay: finished slots idle until the longest request completes.

**Continuous** batching schedules at the **token level**: the moment a request finishes, a queued one takes its slot on the very next step. GPU utilization stays pinned.

steps.title: PagedAttention — virtual memory for the cache
steps.body:
Old servers pre-allocated each request one **contiguous** slab at max length → internal fragmentation, external fragmentation, over-reservation: only **20–40%** of cache memory held real tokens (Kwon et al., SOSP 2023).

vLLM splits the cache into **fixed-size blocks** scattered anywhere, stitched per-request by a **block table** — the OS paging playbook. Blocks allocate only as tokens land; every request draws from one shared pool:

viz.title: Naive vs paged, live
viz.caption: The 'usable pool' knob IS this story — drag it from 40% (naive) to 100% (paged) under load.

steps.title: Prefix caching — compute once, reuse
steps.body:
Requests that share a prefix — the same system prompt, few-shot examples, RAG context, or earlier turns of a chat — **reuse the shared KV blocks** instead of recomputing them. At a 75% hit rate that's ~4× throughput on its own.

All three run in the open-source **vLLM** engine: any model, any accelerator, an OpenAI-compatible API, and a `/metrics` endpoint where you can watch each technique working.

recap: Continuous batching keeps the GPU busy (token-level scheduling). PagedAttention keeps the cache honest (block tables, no fragmentation — recovering the wasted 60–80%). Prefix caching makes shared context free. Together: vLLM, roughly 10× cheaper than naive serving.
